requirements.requirement: Only root and opsadmin are permitted to schedule cron jobs on node1 (via /etc/cron.allow, with no conflicting /etc/cron.deny)
requirements.summary: Baseline showed an empty /etc/cron.deny and no /etc/cron.allow (cmd-93ef9f75ef654bc0). Executor created /etc/cron.allow containing exactly 'root' and 'opsadmin' and removed /etc/cron.deny (cmd-e6b6e851efbb4717). Post-cleanup and post-restart checks both confirm /etc/cron.allow still contains only root+opsadmin and /etc/cron.deny remains absent (cmd-4509c25cb7f34288, cmd-8cc4153213684ace).

requirements.requirement: opsadmin account exists and is able to schedule cron jobs
requirements.summary: opsadmin did not exist at baseline (cmd-0d7aba88dcef473a); created via useradd with uid 1000 (cmd-9e6239d301f44880). Directly demonstrated opsadmin can create and list a crontab entry as itself (cmd-eb3c7cf8ed7d4909), and again post-restart (cmd-8cc4153213684ace).

requirements.requirement: root retains ability to schedule cron jobs
requirements.summary: root successfully created and listed a crontab entry while cron.allow was in effect.

requirements.requirement: Users not listed (root, opsadmin) are denied crontab scheduling
requirements.summary: A third account (testuser), invoking crontab as itself, was directly denied with 'You (testuser) are not allowed to use this program (crontab)', confirming enforcement of the allow-list against a non-listed user.

requirements.requirement: Test artifacts (temporary user, temporary crontab entries) are removed, leaving only the intended configuration
requirements.summary: testuser's crontab and the root/opsadmin test crontabs were removed, active sessions terminated, and testuser deleted; follow-up check confirmed testuser no longer exists and no stray crontabs remain for root/opsadmin (cmd-eaf7862fe51946d7, cmd-17712aa6b2c84afd, cmd-4509c25cb7f34288).

requirements.requirement: Independent provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol (not part of the public task contract, but a supplemental requirement): pre-restart healthy baseline, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, recovered service/config state
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline captured boot_id 31949c21... with crond active (cmd-7830aca8b8dd490c). 'shutdown -r now' was issued in the background and acknowledged immediately (cmd-972882812b2342ac). Connection dropped during reboot (cmd-c17d8c904cd74073, cmd-63211fe929954314, cmd-ef5e1ea4e0ca403a) then recovered with a new boot_id addc7866... (cmd-d611c708f73b4e04). Post-restart check confirms crond active, /etc/cron.allow intact (root+opsadmin only), cron.deny still absent, and opsadmin can still create/list/remove a crontab entry (cmd-8cc4153213684ace). This is independent of the public task contract and does not affect the cron-access-control functionality score, but is used as a confidence and hygiene cross-check.

overall_summary: The task — restricting cron scheduling on node1 to root and opsadmin — is fully and directly satisfied. The executor created the missing opsadmin account, wrote /etc/cron.allow with exactly root and opsadmin, removed the conflicting empty /etc/cron.deny, and proved enforcement both positively (root and opsadmin can create/list crontabs) and negatively (a third test account was denied with the expected cronie error). Test artifacts (testuser, temp crontabs) were fully cleaned up, leaving only the intended configuration, confirmed by a final check. The executor additionally ran the required independent node-restart evidence protocol: a pre-restart healthy baseline, a backgrounded reboot with immediate acknowledgement, a directly observed boot-id change after the connection dropped and recovered, and confirmation that crond, cron.allow, and opsadmin's cron access all survived the reboot. Hygiene is clean; the only residue is a harmless /tmp/reboot.log from the shutdown command.
limitations: Persistence/reboot-survival was not itself part of the public task contract, so while the executor's restart evidence is strong and well-formed, it is treated as supplemental confidence-building rather than a scored material outcome.

No independent confirmation that /etc/cron.allow (rather than some other mechanism) is what RHEL9's cronie build actually consults was captured beyond the observed allow/deny behavior itself; however, the observed denial message is consistent with expected cronie allow-list semantics.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands trace clearly to satisfying the task or the independent restart protocol: creating opsadmin (required by the task), creating/removing a temporary testuser and test crontabs (needed to prove enforcement, fully reverted via crontab -r, loginctl terminate-user, pkill, userdel -r), writing /etc/cron.allow and removing /etc/cron.deny (the core task change), and the single bounded reboot (independent protocol requirement, backgrounded so the ack returned before disconnect). The after-prepare vs after-executor diff shows only the expected boot-id change, ephemeral systemd-private temp dirs regenerated per-boot, sshd/chronyd re-listening with new PIDs after reboot, and one new file /tmp/reboot.log (harmless shutdown-command log, low-risk residue). No failed services, no package-health regressions, and no orphaned test accounts or crontabs remained.
